A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPACeR, with matching research objectives and identifiable corresponding sections, equations, tables, figures and appendices. All comparison-relevant material is readable; internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original WOSAC experiments, reward ablations, planner-evaluation correlations and throughput measurements.

after.justification: v2 reports revised vehicle results and additional pedestrian/cyclist experiments, reference-model sensitivity studies and anchoring analyses.

M1.justification: The stated central alignment objective reverses from KL(reference || policy) to KL(policy || reference) in Sections 3.1–3.2. Whether this corrects v1's description or reflects an implementation change remains unresolved. Independently, v2 introduces a VRU adaptation with agent-type observations, separate action heads and type-specific token vocabularies (Appendix A.1), substantially extending the described method.

E1.justification: WOMD remains the dataset, but coverage expands beyond controlling and evaluating vehicles. v2 additionally trains with vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists controlled together and evaluates pedestrian/cyclist targets separately (Table 2 and Appendix A.1). v1 leaves these road users on logged trajectories.

E2.justification: The vehicle comparison retains PPO, human-regularized PPO, SMART and CAT-K. However, v2 Appendix A.3 explicitly changes HR-PPO from reverse to forward KL and reports the selected variant. Table 1 labels this baseline HF-PPO while the surrounding text retains HR-PPO. This is a substantive revision to one comparator.

E3.justification: New protocols compare 0.3M/1M/3M reference models, 100/200/400-token vocabularies and deterministic top-1 versus stochastic top-5 evaluation. Existing Frenet sampling settings also change, commonly from (15,7,5) to (10,5,3), in v1 Table 4 versus v2 Table A4. Section 4.3 changes the learned-planner count from 22 to 18, although v2 Appendix A.7 still states 22, leaving the exact evaluated set unclear.

E4.justification: v2 adds reference-quality and vocabulary sensitivity analyses (Figure 2), anchoring-weight and sampling analyses (Figure 3), likelihood/KL/entropy training curves (Figure A1), and VRU component ablations (Table A1). These investigate robustness, diversity and component necessity. The original reward-combination ablation is retained as Table A2.

E5.justification: Both versions retain Table 1's ± reporting, the five-seed averaging statement in Section 4.3 and seed 42 in the PPO hyperparameter table. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests or explicit repetition protocol. Changed uncertainty values alone do not establish a different reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises all three RL rows: SPACeR's composite changes from 0.740 to 0.741, minADE from 4.733 to 4.101 and collision rate from 0.020 to 0.036. SMART, CAT-K and throughput results remain unchanged. v2 adds VRU composite scores of 0.729 versus PPO's 0.648 and HR-PPO's 0.668, plus sensitivity and ablation results. Planner correlations also change, including GT–SPACeR PDM correlation from 0.593 to 0.72; revised settings limit direct performance comparisons.

T1.justification: The KL formulation is mathematically revised: the reference-weighted sum and reference/policy log ratio become policy-weighted with the opposite ratio. This is a localized, non-equivalent change to the formal objective. The stochastic-game formulation, conditional-independence factorization and WOSAC metric equations otherwise remain unchanged; no proofs or theorems are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same headline contributions: reference-anchored self-play provides realistic, reactive simulation with competitive WOSAC performance, approximately 10× faster inference and 50× smaller policies. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining their stated scope.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets the reference model as a soft prior that the learned policy can outperform, and explains likelihood-only diversity collapse versus KL-based entropy preservation. VRU discussion changes from an untested extension to demonstrated transfer with pedestrian-specific metric and reward limitations. Section 4.3 also explicitly distinguishes planner-ranking responsiveness from distributional realism.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds implementation information for VRUs, including type indicators, separate action heads and vocabularies. Appendix A.3 documents the HR-PPO KL revision. Most PPO hyperparameters, hardware and reference-training details are retained. The project-website link present in v1's abstract is omitted from v2.

R1.justification: Related work adds broader MARL references, earlier adversarial imitation approaches to driving, and LangTraj: Carroll, Yu, Chen, Kuefler, Bhattacharyya and Chang respectively. The central positioning of an RL-first approach versus imitation-model fine-tuning is retained. Merging the duplicated CAT-K bibliography entries is editorial.

P1.justification: The six main sections and overall argument remain intact. v2 makes localized prose corrections and clarifications, expands experimental discussion, revises acknowledgments and reorganizes the appendix around new VRU and anchoring material. Much existing prose remains unchanged, so the added scientific content does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds three analytical figures and two VRU tables, redraws the planner-correlation chart with reordered legend entries, and relocates the original ablation table to Appendix A.2. The document is also reformatted with conference headers and page numbers. Existing framework and qualitative driving illustrations are retained, rather than representing new case studies.

improvement.justification: v2 replaces v1's untested VRU extension with comparisons and component ablations, while reference-quality and anchoring studies improve understanding of the method's robustness and diversity. These gains are tempered by the unexplained objective reversal, inconsistent planner counts and inaccurate interpretations: the claimed 0.1 vehicle–VRU composite gap conflicts with 0.741 versus 0.729, and Figure 3 shows top-1 degradation at the strongest KL weight. The added evidence improves the paper, but reporting problems limit the overall gain.
